(Corrects paragraph 5 to say softer footfall from adverse weather conditions was since the first half, not in the first half)
March 19 (Reuters) - British sofa retailer DFS Furniture reported a rise in half-year adjusted pretax profit on Thursday, as cost-saving measures and operational efficiencies outweighed challenging macroeconomic conditions and soft demand in the UK.
The company implemented cost cuts and streamlined operations to counter pressure from rising business rates and minimum wages in the UK.
The Doncaster-based company reiterated its full-year adjusted pretax profit forecast of 43 million-50 million pounds ($57.04 million-$66.33 million), supported by these cost-cutting strategies.
However, the company noted that the forecast reiteration assumed no supply chain disruptions from current geo-political events, as retailers grapple with potential supply chain and broader economic headwinds from the conflict in the Middle East.
DFS Furniture said consumer confidence remains "delicately balanced" amid a slowdown in the British economy and persistent inflation and flagged softer footfall from adverse weather conditions since the first half.
The company reported half-year adjusted pretax profit of 30.9 million pounds, in line with previous outlook of 30 million to 31 million pounds.

PLEASANTON, CA / ACCESS Newswire / March 19, 2026 / Armanino Foods of Distinction, Inc. (OTCQX:AMNF), a leading producer and marketer of premium frozen Italian and specialty foods serving foodservice, retail, and industrial customers across North America and select international markets, today reported record financial results for the fourth quarter and full year ended December 31, 2025.
Financial Summary
Fourth Quarter 2025 Highlights:
Net Sales increased 5.5% year-over-year to $19.5 million
Operating Income increased 20.0% to $6.4 million
Operating Margin expanded to 32.8%
Net Income increased 17.3% to $5.1 million, or $0.17 per diluted share
Free Cash Flow of $6.5 million
Full Year 2025 Highlights:
Net Sales increased 9.7% to $76.1 million
Operating Income increased 31.1% to $23.9 million
Operating Margin expanded to 31.4%
Net Income increased 28.0% to $18.7 million, or $0.60 per diluted share
$11.7 million returned to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases
Free Cash Flow of $13.1 million
CEO Commentary
"2025 was a defining year for Armanino Foods," said Deanna Jurgens, President and Chief Executive Officer. "We delivered record performance across every major financial metric - accelerating net sales, expanding margins, and driving more than 30% growth in operating income.

"During the year, we also strengthened our leadership team with experienced executives across finance, operations, growth, national accounts, and international markets. This team is aligned around scalable growth, operational excellence, and disciplined capital allocation.
"As we enter 2026, we are focused on expanding our domestic foodservice business, advancing national account opportunities, and accelerating international expansion, while investing in manufacturing capabilities to support long-term growth."
Fourth Quarter 2025 Performance
Net sales for the fourth quarter increased 5.5% to $19.5 million, reflecting continued demand across the Company's core foodservice and international channels and growth within its expanding sauce portfolio.
Gross profit totaled $9.2 million, or 47.3% of net sales, compared to $9.3 million, or 50.4% of net sales in Q4 2024, which benefited from a favorable adjustment related to trade promotion accruals.
Operating income increased 20.0% to $6.4 million, with operating margin expanding to 32.8%, demonstrating the Company's ability to translate revenue growth into higher profitability through operating leverage and disciplined cost management.
Net income increased 17.3% to $5.1 million, or $0.17 per diluted share. The Company generated $6.5 million in free cash flow during the quarter. Cash and cash equivalents totaled $29.6 million as of December 31, 2025.
Full Year 2025 Performance
For the full year, net sales increased 9.7% to $76.1 million, driven primarily by growth in the Company's foodservice business through high-value customer acquisition, expanded sauce penetration, disciplined trade management, and continued momentum in international markets.
Gross margin expanded 280 basis points to 46.8%, reflecting improvements in product mix, trade optimization, and manufacturing efficiency. Trade spending as a percentage of sales declined compared to the prior year as the Company implemented a more targeted and return-driven commercial strategy.
Operating income increased 31.1% to $23.9 million, with operating margin expanding to 31.4%, demonstrating the scalability of the Company's business model.
Net income increased 28.0% to $18.7 million, or $0.60 per diluted share. Earnings per share growth exceeded net income growth due to the Company's share repurchase program.
The Company generated $13.1 million in free cash flow for the year and returned $11.7 million to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases while maintaining a strong balance sheet with no long-term debt.
Long-term supply agreements secured across core commodity ingredients provide enhanced cost visibility and margin stability entering 2026.

Taipei, March 19 (CNA) Taiwan's central bank on Thursday sharply raised its forecast for growth in Taiwan's gross domestic product (GDP) for 2026 to 7.28 percent, while easing selective credit controls in the home market.
After wrapping up a quarterly policymaking meeting, the central bank said in a statement Taiwan's economy is expected to benefit from a robust export performance and an increase in private investment during the current AI boom to grow 7.28 percent, an upgrade from the previous estimate of 3.67 percent made in December.
The upgrade is in line with the Directorate General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics (DGBAS), which raised its forecast for Taiwan's GDP growth in 2026 from 3.54 percent in November to 7.71 percent in February.
The central bank said that while the government has cut commodity taxes for select goods, with service cost growth likely to continue to moderate, the war in the Middle East has pushed up international crude oil prices, which could complicate local consumer prices.
By taking into account government price stabilization measures to cap energy prices, the central bank said it has raised the 2026 consumer price index (CPI) growth forecast from 1.63 percent to 1.80 percent and also increased the forecast for core CPI, which excludes vegetables, fruit and energy, from 1.63 percent to 1.75 percent.
After the hikes, CPI and core CPI growth are still below the 2 percent alert level set by the central bank.
At the policymaking meeting, the bank decided to leave its key interest rates unchanged for the eighth consecutive quarter, citing stable inflation.
The central bank said the decision also took into account uncertainties created by the military conflict in the Middle East and the U.S. tariff policies.
After the decision, Taiwan's discount rate remains at 2 percent, still the highest level in 15 years, with the rate on accommodations with collateral at 2.375 percent and the rate on accommodations without collateral at 4.250 percent.
Meanwhile, the central bank said following its imposition of a seventh round of credit control measures on the home market in September 2024 to rein in home prices, credit controls will now be partially eased.
Starting from Friday, the loan-to-value ratio -- the percentage of the value of a home that can be carried in a mortgage -- for individual buyers for their second-home mortgages will be raised from 50 percent to 60 percent.
Despite the easing of the loan-to-value ratio, the central bank said no grace period is allowed for individual buyers who already own a home but will buy a second one, which means they will be required to pay interest and the principal at the same time.
After a series of selective credit control measures, home mortgages extended by Taiwanese banks accounted for 36.0 percent of their total lending at the end of February, from a high of 37.6 percent at the end of June 2024, the central bank said.
In addition, the growth of banks' aggregate lending to the property market also fell to 3.7 percent at the end of February from a high of 9.4 percent as of the end of September 2024, the central bank added.
The bank said it will continue to monitor the local property market and review the effects of its selective credit control measures to stabilize local financial markets and improve the operations of the banking sector.

Top 10 Secrets for Mega Profits with Synthetic Position Arbitrage: The Ultimate 2026 Investor’s Guide to Risk-Free Wealth
In the sophisticated world of derivatives trading, the ability to replicate the risk and reward profile of an asset without actually holding it is the ultimate hallmark of a professional. Synthetic position arbitrage is not merely a trading technique; it is a mathematical discipline that exploits the structural inefficiencies of the financial markets to lock in low-risk or risk-neutral profits. As we navigate the complex trading environment of 2026, where high-frequency algorithms and AI-driven liquidity dominate, understanding the nuance of synthetic construction is the key to achieving alpha that remains uncorrelated with broader market direction.
The following list summarizes the ten most effective synthetic arbitrage techniques used by institutional desks and elite quant traders to extract consistent gains from the options market.
- The Classic Conversion: A delta-neutral strategy where a trader buys the underlying stock and offsets it with a synthetic short position (selling a call and buying a put) to capture overpriced call premiums.
- The Reversal (Reverse Conversion): Exploiting overpriced puts or high interest rate environments by shorting the stock and creating a synthetic long position through options.
- Risk-Free Box Spreads: A four-legged strategy that combines a bull vertical call spread and a bear vertical put spread to replicate a fixed-interest loan or deposit, capturing interest rate mispricings.
- The Long Jelly Roll: An inter-temporal arbitrage that profits from discrepancies in the cost-of-carry and time decay (theta) between different expiration cycles.
- Synthetic Dividend Capture: Using conversions to profit when the options market misprices the expected dividend payout of a stock relative to the actual corporate distribution.
- Hard-to-Borrow (HTB) Synthesis: Replicating a short stock position with options to avoid the exorbitant borrowing fees and regulatory constraints (Reg-SHO) of physically shorting a “locate-restricted” security.
- Delta-Neutral Volatility Arbitrage: Exploiting the gap between an option’s implied volatility (IV) and the underlying asset’s realized volatility (RV) without taking a directional bet on price.
- Cross-Market/Regional Arbitrage: Identifying pricing gaps between a security’s synthetic options equivalent on one exchange and its spot or futures price on another regional exchange.
- Section 1256 Tax Arbitrage: Leveraging the 60/40 tax treatment of index-based synthetic positions to achieve higher net-of-tax returns compared to standard equity trades.
- Gamma Scalping in Synthetic Straddles: Extracting profits from small price oscillations while maintaining neutrality through the constant rebalancing of a synthetic straddle construction.
The Mathematical Bedrock: Put-Call Parity and the Law of One Price
The efficacy of every synthetic arbitrage technique rests upon a foundational principle of financial mathematics known as put-call parity. This principle defines the absolute relationship that must exist between call prices, put prices, the underlying spot price, and the present value of the strike price for options of the same class, strike, and expiration.
In a frictionless market, two assets that provide the same future payoff must trade at the same price. If they do not, an arbitrageur can sell the expensive asset and buy the cheaper one, locking in the difference as profit. For European options, this relationship is expressed by the standard formula:

The Role of Cost of Carry ()
In professional environments, the formula is expanded to include the “Reversal/Conversion” value or Cost of Carry ( ). This component accounts for the financing costs of holding the stock and the impact of dividends paid during the holding period. The refined equation used on trading desks is:

When market forces cause or to drift away from this equality, the “parity” is violated, and an arbitrage window opens.
Synthetic Replication Ratios
Traders use these relationships to create “synthetic” versions of any position. A synthetic long stock position, for example, is created by buying a call and selling a put at the same strike price. This mimics the risk-reward profile of the stock with significantly lower capital requirements.

The primary driver behind these constructions is capital efficiency. Replicating a $2,500 position in a stock like Reliance through a synthetic long might require only a fraction of the margin required for an outright purchase, thereby magnifying the potential return on capital.
1. The Classic Conversion: Locking in Credits
A conversion is the most fundamental arbitrage strategy, designed to exploit situations where call options are overpriced relative to puts and the underlying. This often occurs when bullish sentiment is extreme, and demand for call options drives premiums to a level that violates parity.
To execute a conversion, the trader performs three simultaneous actions:
- Purchase the underlying stock (100 shares per contract).
- Sell an at-the-money or near-the-money call option.
- Purchase a put option with the same strike price and expiration as the call.
The result is a delta-neutral position. The profit is locked in at the moment of execution and is equal to the net credit received from the options minus the difference between the stock purchase price and the strike price.
Strategic Insight: Institutional traders often use conversions to “capture the dividend.” If the market underprices the probability or size of a dividend, the conversion allows the trader to own the stock and collect the dividend while the synthetic short position (long put + short call) protects them from any price fluctuations in the underlying.
2. The Reversal: Capitalizing on Downside Demand
A reversal, or reverse conversion, is the mirror image of a conversion. It is deployed when put options are overpriced, typically during periods of market fear or high demand for portfolio hedging.
The reversal setup involves:
- Short-selling the underlying stock.
- Purchasing a call option.
- Selling a put option with the same strike and expiration.
The core profitability of a reversal often comes from the interest earned on the cash proceeds of the short sale. When a trader short-sells stock, the cash is held by the broker, and in a high-interest-rate environment (like that projected for 2026), the interest earned on this balance can be significant. If the put premium is high enough to offset the cost of the call, the interest becomes pure profit.
The Rebate Rate Factor: A critical nuance in reversals is the “rebate rate.” This is the interest rate the short-seller receives on the cash collateral. If a stock is “hard-to-borrow,” the rebate rate can drop to zero or even become negative, meaning the trader must pay to short the stock. In such cases, the reversal may only be profitable if the put premium is excessively high relative to the call.
3. Risk-Free Box Spreads: The Quant’s Synthetic Loan
A box spread is an advanced arbitrage strategy that removes all directional bias and focuses purely on interest rates and pricing efficiency. It is composed of four options: a bull call spread and a bear put spread using the same two strike prices and expiration date.
The Anatomy of a Box Spread
- Long Call Spread: Buy Call at Strike A, Sell Call at Strike B.
- Long Put Spread: Buy Put at Strike B, Sell Put at Strike A.
Regardless of where the stock price ends at expiration, the value of a box spread will always be equal to the difference between the two strike prices.

If the total cost to enter the box is less than the present value of that $10.00 payoff, an arbitrage opportunity exists. In 2026, many traders use the “Short Box” to borrow money at rates lower than traditional margin, while institutional desks “Buy Boxes” to park excess cash at rates superior to Treasury bills.
Risk Warning: Box spreads should generally only be executed with European-style options (like SPX or other index options) to avoid the risk of early assignment on the short legs, which could dismantle the “risk-free” structure of the trade.
4. The Long Jelly Roll: Inter-Temporal Theta Capture
The long jelly roll is a sophisticated strategy that exploits pricing discrepancies between two different expiration months for the same strike price. It essentially combines a synthetic long position in one month with a synthetic short position in a later month.
Construction Steps
- Month 1 (Near-term): Create a long calendar spread by buying a call and selling a put.
- Month 2 (Far-term): Create a short calendar spread by selling a call and buying a put.
The goal of the jelly roll is to capture the difference in time decay (theta) between the near-term and far-term synthetic positions. This strategy is particularly effective when the market misprices the “cost of carry” over time, allowing the trader to lock in a gain regardless of the underlying asset’s direction.
Market Neutrality: Because the strategy involves equal and opposite positions at the same strike price, it is entirely market-neutral. Its success depends solely on the convergence of the mispriced time-value components.
5. Synthetic Dividend Capture: Profiting from Corporate Payouts
Dividend arbitrage is a specialized form of the conversion strategy. Stock dividends are priced into the options market—specifically, call premiums tend to decrease and put premiums tend to increase as the ex-dividend date approaches.
Arbitrageurs look for discrepancies where the market is pricing in a dividend that is lower than what the company is actually expected to pay. By executing a conversion (Buy Stock, Sell Call, Buy Put), the trader receives the actual dividend while the synthetic short position hedges the stock price movement.

This strategy requires precise timing and deep research into corporate announcements and historical payout ratios, as even a small error in the projected dividend can turn a profitable arbitrage into a losing trade.
6. Hard-to-Borrow (HTB) Synthesis: Bypassing Short Restrictions
Short-selling a stock that is “hard-to-borrow” can be prohibitively expensive due to high borrowing rates and the constant threat of a “buy-in” under Reg-SHO. Synthetic shorting provides an elegant solution to these constraints.
A synthetic short (Long Put + Short Call) mimics the payout of shorting the stock without the need to actually borrow shares. However, the market is usually efficient; when a stock becomes hard-to-borrow, put premiums typically rise and call premiums fall to reflect the borrowing costs.
Strategic Edge: The arbitrage opportunity arises when the synthetic short is cheaper than the cost of physically borrowing the stock. By monitoring the “rebate rate spread,” traders can identify when the options market has not yet fully adjusted to the difficulty of shorting a particular security, allowing them to establish a short position at a significant discount.
7. Delta-Neutral Volatility Arbitrage: Trading the “Fear Gap”
Volatility arbitrage is a statistical strategy that seeks to profit from the difference between the Implied Volatility (IV) of an option and the Realized Volatility (RV) of the underlying asset.
Mechanics of the Trade
A trader identifies an option where IV is significantly higher or lower than the expected RV. To isolate the volatility component, the trader creates a delta-neutral portfolio:
- If IV < Expected RV: Buy the option (long volatility) and hedge the delta by selling the underlying stock.
- If IV > Expected RV: Sell the option (short volatility) and hedge by buying the underlying.
Continuous Rebalancing: Delta is not static; it changes as the stock price moves and as time passes (a second-order effect known as Gamma). Professional arbitrageurs use automated systems to rebalance their stock hedges as the delta drifts, ensuring the position remains insensitive to price direction while extracting profits from the volatility mispricing.
8. Cross-Market/Regional Arbitrage: Exploiting Global Gaps
In the globalized markets of 2026, many securities trade on multiple exchanges or have highly correlated counterparts across regions (e.g., an Indian stock and its ADR in the US, or a spot index and its futures).
Triangular and cross-market arbitrage involves:
- Identifying a price discrepancy between the synthetic version of an asset on one exchange and its physical price on another.
- Simultaneously buying the cheaper version and selling the more expensive version.
Infrastructure Requirements: This strategy is unforgiving. To be successful, traders must use instititutional-grade infrastructure, including co-located servers (e.g., in data centers like NY4 or LD4) and FIX API connections to ensure execution speeds measured in microseconds.
9. Section 1256 Tax Arbitrage: The “Hidden” Profit
For US-based traders, the tax treatment of a trade can be just as important as the trade itself. Arbitrageurs often choose between individual equity options and broad-based index options (like SPX, NDX, or RUT) specifically for the tax benefits.
Under IRS Section 1256, gains on index-based synthetic positions are taxed at a blended 60/40 rate:
- 60% at the lower long-term capital gains rate.
- 40% at the short-term capital gains rate.

By structuring an arbitrage trade (like a box spread) using 1256-eligible contracts, a trader can instantly boost their net profitability by over 10% simply through tax efficiency.
10. Gamma Scalping in Synthetic Straddles
Gamma scalping is the ultimate strategy for “sideways” or “oscillating” markets. A trader creates a synthetic straddle (buying two calls and selling one stock contract, or buying two puts and buying one stock contract) to achieve a delta-neutral position with Positive Gamma.
The Profit Engine
- As the stock price rises, the positive gamma causes the delta to become positive. The trader then sells shares to return to delta-neutrality.
- As the stock price falls, the delta becomes negative, and the trader buys shares to rebalance.
This process of “selling high and buying low” through the rebalancing of the delta hedge creates a stream of small profits that can offset the time decay (theta) of the options. This is a “volatility play” that relies on the stock moving back and forth within a range.
2026 Execution: The Reality of Slippage and Infrastructure
While the mathematics of synthetic arbitrage are perfect, the execution is not. In 2026, the primary obstacles for traders are transaction costs, liquidity, and the speed of institutional algorithms.
The “Alligator Spread” Dilemma
In the retail world, multi-legged strategies like box spreads are often called “alligator spreads” because commissions can devour the entire profit. For example, if a box spread offers a theoretical $0.50 profit per share, but your broker charges $1.00 per contract per leg, your total commission for the four legs is $4.00, which is eight times the theoretical profit.

To compete, modern traders are moving toward Portfolio Margining, which aligns the required collateral with the actual net risk of the portfolio rather than the gross size of the positions. This allows for much higher leverage on delta-neutral arbitrage strategies, turning small pricing anomalies into significant returns.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)
What is the biggest risk in synthetic arbitrage?
While these strategies are often called “risk-free,” the biggest practical risk is execution risk and early assignment risk. In a conversion or box spread, if one of your short options is exercised early, your delta-neutral hedge is broken, leaving you with an unintended directional position that can lead to massive losses.
Why is put-call parity more reliable with European options?
European options can only be exercised at expiration, whereas American options can be exercised at any time. This flexibility introduces “Early Exercise Risk,” which can disrupt an arbitrage structure. For this reason, professional box spreads and reversals are almost exclusively traded on European-style index options like SPX or NDX.
How do I identify a hard-to-borrow stock for synthesis?
Traders look at the Rebate Rate Spread. When the interest you receive on your short sale proceeds is significantly lower than the risk-free rate (or even negative), the stock is hard-to-borrow. At this point, synthetic shorting via options often becomes more cost-effective than physical shorting.
Does AI play a role in synthetic arbitrage in 2026?
Yes. Brokers now use AI to detect arbitrage patterns and adjust their quotes to eliminate spreads in milliseconds. Conversely, traders use AI agents to scan thousands of strike combinations and regional markets to find micro-inefficiencies that last for only a few seconds.
What is the difference between Strategy-Based and Portfolio Margin?
Strategy-based margin (Reg-T) calculates requirements based on set formulas for each position (e.g., a spread), ignoring other offsetting hedges in the account. Portfolio Margin uses models like OCC’s TIMS to simulate market moves and set margin levels based on the actual net risk, often requiring 70-80% less capital for arbitrage strategies.
Can I use synthetic positions to hedge an existing stock portfolio?
Absolutely. A “Synthetic Put” (Short Stock + Long Call) or a “Protective Put” (Long Stock + Long Put) can protect your portfolio from downside moves while maintaining exposure to potential gains.
How does theta decay impact these strategies?
Theta, or time decay, is a friend to the short-option trader and an enemy to the long-option trader. In delta-neutral strategies, the goal is often to ensure that the theta earned from short positions offsets any premium paid, or that the arbitrage credit itself is large enough to cover the “cost” of time.
The 2026 Outlook: Tokenization and 24/7 Liquidity
As we move into the latter half of the decade, two major trends are redefining synthetic arbitrage: Tokenization and 24/7 Trading.
The tokenization of private equity, treasuries, and real estate is creating new “synthetic equivalents” that trade on digital ledgers. This allows for arbitrage between traditional equity markets and their digital-twin counterparts. Furthermore, the shift toward 24/7 trading means that arbitrage windows no longer open only at the “opening bell”; instead, information moves continuously, and pricing gaps are filled by AI agents that operate around the clock.
Winning in 2026 requires a move away from manual “guesswork” and toward a modular, data-driven approach. By mastering the ten synthetic arbitrage techniques outlined in this report and leveraging institutional-grade infrastructure, investors can move beyond directional bets and achieve a level of profit that is truly independent of market cycles.

7 Best Sustainable Derivative Investments to Maximize ESG Returns in 2026: The Ultimate Strategic Guide to Explosive Green Growth
The following list identifies the most sophisticated and high-performing sustainable derivative instruments currently available for institutional and professional investors looking to capitalize on the USD 45.61 trillion ESG investing market as it moves into the 2026 fiscal year.
- CORSIA-Eligible Carbon Futures: These represent the apex of the converging voluntary and compliance carbon markets, serving as essential hedging tools for the aviation sector as it enters Phase I of the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation.
- Sustainability-Linked Interest Rate Swaps (SLDs): These instruments integrate environmental, social, and governance Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) directly into the margin grid of interest rate hedges, often providing 5-10 basis point discounts for meeting verifiable sustainability targets.
- E-mini S&P 500 ESG Index Futures: Traded on the CME Group, these are the most liquid ESG equity index futures globally, allowing for cost-effective exposure to best-in-class ESG performers while systematically excluding controversial sectors like tobacco and thermal coal.
- Afforestation, Reforestation, and Revegetation (ARR) Swaps: Nature-based removal derivatives that command a structural quality premium, with high-integrity BBB+ rated projects trading at multiples significantly higher than legacy avoidance credits.
- Physical Climate Risk and Catastrophe (CAT) Derivatives: Increasingly critical for hedging against the USD 220 billion in annual climate-related asset damage, these swaps focus on adaptation and resilience infrastructure rather than simple emissions reduction.
- Green Bond Index Futures: Based on the Bloomberg MSCI Global Green Bond Index, these derivatives allow fixed-income managers to hedge the interest rate risk of ring-fenced environmental projects while maintaining exposure to the burgeoning USD 1.22 trillion green debt market.
- Renewable Energy Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) Proxies: Synthetic derivatives that manage price volatility for solar and wind energy production, critical as renewable infrastructure becomes the foundational pillar of the net-zero economy.
The Macroeconomic Context of Sustainable Finance in 2026
The global landscape of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) investing has matured from a niche ethical consideration into a structural necessity for global capital markets. As of 2026, the global ESG investing market size is valued at approximately USD 45.61 trillion, with projections suggesting it will reach a staggering USD 180.78 trillion by 2034, exhibiting a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 18.80%. This growth is not merely a reflection of increased capital flow but a fundamental recalibration of how risk and value are assessed in a world where physical climate impacts have reached critical thresholds. In 2026, sustainable finance is defined by “steely pragmatism,” focusing on the material financial implications of labor practices, supply-chain resilience, and environmental liabilities.
The year 2026 marks a “show me” period for the industry, where companies and asset managers must deliver measurable returns and verifiable outcomes. The initial wave of “greenwashing” has been met with a sophisticated regulatory response, including the EU’s Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) and the formal adoption of International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) frameworks across nearly 40 jurisdictions. While some political backtracking has occurred in the United States, with the SEC retreating from its federal climate-risk disclosure rule defense, regional mandates like California’s SB 253 and SB 261 ensure that large-scale corporate transparency remains a requirement for those operating in the world’s fifth-largest economy.

The Transformation of Carbon Credit Futures: Quality, Integrity, and Convergence
The carbon market in 2026 has entered a phase of structural professionalization, characterized by a distinct “flight to quality.” The fragmentation of the previous decade has been replaced by a market tiered by integrity, methodology, and durability. The total carbon market value, estimated at USD 887 billion in 2025, is projected to reach USD 1.22 trillion in 2026, driven by stricter corporate net-zero targets and the implementation of Article 6 of the Paris Agreement.
The convergence of voluntary and compliance markets is the most significant trend for carbon derivatives in 2026. Article 6.4 mechanisms, clarified during COP30 in November 2025, have established a pipeline for Internationally Transferred Mitigation Outcomes (ITMOs), effectively allowing credits to be used across jurisdictional borders for both voluntary commitments and compliance obligations. This has created a robust secondary market for carbon futures on major exchanges like ICE and EEX, where European Union Allowance (EUA) and California Carbon Allowance (CCA) contracts serve as global benchmarks.
The Structural Quality Premium in Carbon Offsetting
Data from Sylvera and other rating agencies highlight a widening price spread between high-integrity and legacy carbon credits. As of late 2025, BBB+ rated Afforestation, Reforestation, and Revegetation (ARR) projects reached median prices above USD 35 per tonne of CO2 equivalent (tCO2e), while lower-rated nature-based projects struggled to find buyers at prices below USD 20. This “quality premium” is no longer rhetorical but is fully priced into the 2026 market, as institutional buyers utilize granular data to evaluate monitoring, reporting, and verification (MRV) robustness, permanence mechanisms, and community safeguards.

This tightening drives higher prices for top-tier credits and incentivizes the use of long-term offtake agreements as a strategic procurement tool.
CORSIA and Compliance-Linked Demand
The aviation sector has become a primary driver of the carbon derivative market through the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA). As CORSIA Phase I (2024-2026) reaches its final year, airlines are mandated to purchase eligible credits for emissions exceeding 85% of their 2019 baseline. Dec-2026 and Dec-2027 futures for CORSIA-eligible credits have traded around USD 16, a price point that many analysts consider an artificially weak demand signal. There is a broad expectation that as compliance obligations are enforced, the mispricing of these futures will correct, creating a rapid upside for project developers who can bring CORSIA-eligible volumes to market.
Strategic Hedging with Sustainability-Linked Derivatives (SLDs)
Sustainability-linked derivatives represent the intersection of conventional risk management and active ESG impact. These instruments add an ESG-linked pricing component to standard hedging contracts like interest rate swaps (IRS), cross-currency swaps, or forwards. Unlike “use-of-proceeds” green bonds, SLDs are highly customizable and utilize specific Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) to set non-financial targets that have direct financial consequences for the counterparty.
The core mechanism of an SLD is the margin adjustment based on KPI achievement. For example, a corporation might enter into an interest rate swap where the fixed rate is reduced if the company achieves a specific reduction in Scope 1 greenhouse gas emissions or improves its gender diversity score as verified by an independent agency like Sustainalytics.
Financial Incentive Structures and KPI Guidelines
The market has seen a variety of incentive structures, ranging from spread discounts to penalty-based payments. In the case of SBM Offshore’s 2019 Sustainability Improvement Derivative—the world’s first of its kind—the firm received a 5-10 basis point discount on its fixed rate for meeting target ESG scores, but faced a 5-10 basis point penalty for failure. Other structures involve charitable donations; for instance, Siemens Gamesa executed an IRS where changes in the ESG rating prompted donations to non-profits by either the bank (on improvement) or the company (on decline).

Equity Index Derivatives: Liquid Exposure and Factor Performance
Equity index futures and options tied to ESG benchmarks have become the dominant vehicle for institutional managers seeking to allocate capital efficiently without managing individual stock portfolios. These derivatives enable the implementation of ESG strategies in a cost-effective manner while providing better liquidity than direct underlying stock investment.
The CME Group’s E-mini S&P 500 ESG Index futures (ESG) have emerged as the most liquid ESG equity index futures globally, with significant growth in average daily volume (ADV). The underlying index selects constituents with high ESG scores and medium ESG momentum while avoiding the worst-scoring firms. This strategy has allowed the S&P 500 ESG Index to consistently outperform or match its traditional counterpart, particularly in volatile markets.
The Role of Eurex and Euronext in ESG Benchmarking
European exchanges have led the initial development of these products. Eurex established derivatives on the STOXX ESG-X Factor Indices, which exclude companies involved in weapons, tobacco, and thermal coal. They also offer “ESG Enhanced Focus” versions of MSCI benchmarks for global regions including Japan and the Emerging Markets. Euronext launched the Euronext ESG80 Index, which tracks 80 companies supporting a low-carbon transition while excluding firms with poor social and governance assessments.

The Rise of Physical Climate Risk and Adaptation Finance
A fundamental shift in the 2026 investment landscape is the pivot from climate mitigation to adaptation and resilience. With the average global temperature having likely exceeded the 1.5°C threshold in the 2023-2025 period, markets are now pricing physical climate risks—such as heat stress, water scarcity, and coastal flooding—directly into asset valuations, insurance costs, and credit risk.
Physical climate risk is estimated to have cost hundreds of billions of dollars per year by 2025, and by 2050, as much as USD 28.3 trillion of global GDP could be at risk. Consequently, climate adaptation finance is aiming to triple to USD 120 billion annually by 2035. This reality has moved physical risk from a compliance consideration to a core value driver for global banks and investors.
Hedging Asset Damage and Infrastructure Resilience
Investors are increasingly utilizing weather derivatives and catastrophe (CAT) swaps to manage these physical exposures. For instance, modeled physical asset-damage risk has been shown to increase the weighted average cost of capital (WACC) by 22 basis points for every 10-percentage-point increase in modeled risk. Large municipal bonds, such as those in Los Angeles, are already seeing the pricing impact of physical risks like wildfires.

The AI-Energy Nexus and Sustainable Infrastructure
The emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) as a dominant economic force has created a unique “AI-energy nexus” that sustainable investors must navigate. In 2026, the scramble for energy to support data center build-outs has propelled global investment activity, but it also demands that the industry deliver verifiable outcomes in terms of efficiency and productivity.
Major tech companies like NVIDIA, Microsoft, and IDEXX Laboratories are frequently cited as the standard-bearers for sustainable technology. NVIDIA’s Blackwell GPUs are reportedly more than 50 times more energy efficient than traditional CPUs for large language model inference workloads, and the company achieved 100% renewable electricity for its global offices in fiscal 2025. Similarly, Microsoft has committed to a zero-waste goal, diverting 26,000 metric tons of waste from landfills across its data centers.
Renewable Energy Infrastructure as a Core Holding
Renewable energy infrastructure—wind, solar, and storage—has become the foundation of the net-zero economy. Companies like Ørsted, which transitioned from fossil fuels to offshore wind leadership, symbolize this evolution. Institutional investors favor direct stakes in these assets because they provide predictable, inflation-linked returns. By 2026, solar energy has become the main source of electricity growth globally, despite geopolitical headwinds such as trade tensions and changes in government subsidy mechanisms in China and the United States.

These instruments are favored by investors because they provide “ring-fenced” capital for projects with measurable environmental outcomes. The market size for green bonds is projected to expand at a high-single-digit pace through 2031, supported by sovereign, municipal, and supranational issuers.

Navigating Regulatory Fragmentation in 2026
As of 2026, the regulatory landscape for sustainable finance is characterized by a “fragmented and dynamic” environment, with significant divergence between jurisdictions. The EU continues to lead with mandatory reporting obligations under the CSRD and CSDDD, though these were simplified in 2025 to raise revenue and employee thresholds, effectively removing 90% of smaller companies from the reporting scope to focus on the largest entities.
In the United States, the regulatory environment has become significantly more complex. The SEC’s Biden-era climate-risk disclosure rule is currently in “limbo” after the agency abandoned its legal defense in late 2025. SEC Chair Paul Atkins has pivoted toward a “principles-based” approach, focused on reducing the cost of public ownership. However, state-level mandates are filling the gap; California’s SB 253 requires greenhouse gas reporting for entities with over USD 1 billion in revenue, with initial Scope 1 and 2 disclosures due by June 30, 2026.
SFDR Articles 8 and 9: Transparency and Governance
The EU’s Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation (SFDR) remains the global anchor for fund classification. Article 8 funds (“light green”) are those that promote environmental or social characteristics, while Article 9 funds (“dark green”) have sustainable investment as their core objective. Both require investee companies to follow “good governance” practices, though the interpretation of what constitutes good governance is still largely left to fund managers. By 2026, the SFDR classification has become a primary tool for combating greenwashing and establishing a transparent “playing field” for investors.

Synthesis: Professional Recommendations for 2026
The convergence of climate risk, technological advancement, and regulatory maturity has created a new era for sustainable derivatives. Investors who leverage the professionalization of the carbon market, the strategic flexibility of SLDs, and the resilience focus of adaptation finance will be best positioned to capture the outperformance of the ESG sector. In 2026, success is defined by a move from venture risk toward infrastructure returns, where transparency, data-driven analysis, and verifiable impact are the primary metrics of value.
Strategic Roadmap for ESG Allocation
- Carbon Portfolios: Prioritize high-integrity credits with BBB+ Sylvera ratings and CORSIA-eligible removals to avoid the pricing “dead zone” of oversupplied legacy credits.
- Corporate Treasury: Integrate SLDs into revolving credit facilities to achieve direct margin benefits linked to Scope 1-3 reduction targets.
- Equity Allocation: Utilize highly liquid index futures like the E-mini S&P 500 ESG to maintain core market exposure while managing factor risk and ethical alignment.
- Risk Management: Pivot toward “adaptation and resilience” by incorporating weather derivatives and CAT swaps into broader portfolio construction to hedge increasing physical asset-damage costs.
- Technological Alignment: Focus on “AI-energy efficiency” by investing in infrastructure leaders who provide the power-per-watt optimization necessary for the carbon-constrained growth of 2026.
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)
What is the “greenium” in sustainable bond markets? The “greenium” refers to the slightly lower yield (and thus higher price) that investors are willing to accept for a green bond compared to a non-green bond of the same issuer, due to high demand for labeled debt. In 2026, rising interest rates have moderately eroded this premium, though it remains relevant for high-quality EU GBS-compliant issues.
How do Article 6 mechanisms impact my carbon credit investment? Article 6.4 of the Paris Agreement provides the legal framework for the international transfer of carbon credits (ITMOs). This allows credits to be used for national NDC targets as well as voluntary corporate goals, significantly increasing the potential pool of buyers and creating a more robust, standardized global price for carbon.
Why is there a focus on “Physical Risk” over “Transition Risk” in 2026? As global temperatures breach the 1.5°C threshold, the “Transition” phase (policy changes) has been partially overtaken by the “Physical” phase (actual weather-related damage). Investors are shifting focus to adaptation—protecting assets from damage—because these risks are now more immediate and financially material than the pace of future regulation.
What are CORSIA-eligible credits? These are specific carbon credits that meet the rigorous standards set by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO). Airlines must use these credits to offset emissions above their baseline under the CORSIA scheme, making them “anchor buyers” for high-integrity credits in 2026.
How do I differentiate between Article 8 and Article 9 funds? Article 8 funds promote environmental/social characteristics but may have other primary financial objectives. Article 9 funds have sustainable investment as their primary objective and must have a non-financial objective at the core of their offering. Both are viewed as ESG-aligned, but Article 9 is considered the “dark green” or highest intensity category.

Bitcoin's recent price action confirms a major technical shift. The asset was rejected at $76,000, a level it had tested for two straight years. This rejection solidifies the area as significant resistance, capping a prolonged rally and signaling a potential reversal in momentum.
The bounce from that rejection has been supported by strong institutional flows. Since early March, Bitcoin ETF inflows have exceeded $1.9 billion. This sustained demand has helped absorb selling pressure during macro-driven pullbacks, providing a fundamental floor for the price.
On-chain data reveals a key accumulation signal. Despite the price decline, Bitcoin balances on centralized exchanges dropped by approximately 12,400 BTC over a recent period. This outflow brings total exchange reserves to a 12% drop from recent highs, indicating holders are moving coins off exchanges-often a sign of long-term holding or strategic accumulation ahead of a potential supply squeeze.
Institutional Accumulation vs. Panic
The market is split between two narratives. On one side, retail sentiment is in full retreat, with the Crypto Fear & Greed Index at 16 (Extreme Fear). This is a level not seen since February, signaling deep pessimism among smaller traders. On the other, on-chain data shows a steady accumulation of by larger, more strategic players.
This divergence is clear in the liquidity and price action. Despite the fear, the market maintains healthy flow, with Bitcoin's volume-to-market-cap ratio at 8.1%. This indicates that trading activity is robust relative to the asset's size, preventing a panic sell-off. More importantly, Bitcoin's price has held up against the broader market's weakness. While the crypto market cap has been volatile, Bitcoin has outperformed its peers, with altcoins experiencing median declines of 4-6%. This defensive strength underscores Bitcoin's role as a relative safe haven.
The bottom line is a classic flow war. Retail traders are fleeing at extreme fear levels, but institutional accumulation is absorbing that selling. The evidence points to a supply squeeze forming, as exchange reserves dropped by approximately 12,400 BTC during the recent pullback. This outflow from central exchanges, coupled with large wallets increasing their holdings, suggests that the "smart money" is buying the dip. The price action will hinge on which side of this flow war gains momentum.

The current setup is fragile, with the Fear & Greed index at 16 (Extreme Fear) and the ADX at 51.3, signaling a strong bearish trend. The bounce remains vulnerable to a breakdown.

Capital Shift: Bitcoin ETF Outflows Fuel Stablecoin Digital Dollar Surge
Penny McCormerReviewed by
Shunan Liu
The capital is moving, but in opposite directions. On one side, the stablecoin ecosystem is experiencing explosive growth, with monthly transaction volume hitting a record $1.8 trillion in February. USDC has become the dominant player, accounting for 70% of all stablecoin transfer volume and even overtaking Tether in trading volume despite its smaller market cap. This surge in usage, driven by rapid minting, signals a massive shift toward a digital dollar for everyday transactions and liquidity.
On the flip side, the flow into is drying up. Over the past five weeks, investors have withdrawn nearly $3.8 billion from U.S.-listed spot Bitcoin ETFs, marking the longest outflow streak since early 2025. This persistent selling, led by BlackRock's IBIT, reflects a clear retreat from the volatile asset class by institutional players.
The divergence is stark. While billions are being parked in the stablecoin digital dollar for its utility and stability, a similar amount is being pulled from the core crypto asset. This capital is not disappearing; it's simply shifting from the high-risk, high-reward Bitcoin ETFs into the more stable, transaction-focused world of stablecoins.
The Mechanics: Deleveraging and Liquidity Restoration
The immediate driver behind Bitcoin's sharp 19% drawdown was a forced reduction in market leverage. Over the past week, futures open interest fell from roughly $61 billion to about $49 billion, a decline of more than 20% in notional exposure. This rapid unwind, while orderly, created a tail-event price move, with Bitcoin registering a -6.05σ drop on February 5. The selling pressure was significant but not a full capitulation, as total liquidations were estimated at $2 to $2.5 billion in Bitcoin futures.
This deleveraging is directly linked to the surge in stablecoin liquidity. As Bitcoin's leverage unwound, a massive pool of buying power was being built on exchanges. The record $1.8 trillion in monthly stablecoin transaction volume in February reflects this shift, with USDC alone accounting for 70% of that flow. More critically, over $3 billion in USDC has been minted already in March, with supply on exchanges rising to a three-week high. This influx provides a direct source of funds for crypto purchases.
The capital flow is a de-risking move, not a complete exit from digital assets. Investors are pulling money from volatile Bitcoin ETFs and using the proceeds to mint stablecoins, which are then parked on exchanges. This creates a two-pronged effect: it reduces systemic risk by lowering leverage, while simultaneously building a large, ready-to-spend pool of digital dollars. As the stablecoin supply ratio (SSR) shows a recovery, it signals that this liquidity is returning to the market, potentially forming the foundation for a future upswing.
Catalysts and Risks: What to Watch for the Next Move
The path forward hinges on two opposing flows. The primary catalyst for a Bitcoin recovery is a reversal in the institutional exodus from ETFs. Sustained inflows, not just a pause, are needed to re-engage the capital that has been pulled. The current five-week outflow streak of nearly $3.8 billion shows persistent wariness, with BlackRock's IBIT leading the retreat. A shift from this pattern would signal a return of institutional conviction.
A key risk is that the stablecoin liquidity engine sputters. The record $1.8 trillion in monthly transaction volume and rapid USDC minting are building a pool of digital dollars ready to buy. If this growth plateaus, it caps the available buying power for a crypto market upswing. The market's recovery potential is directly tied to the continued expansion of this stablecoin supply on exchanges.
For traders, the shift in Bitcoin's funding rates is a critical early warning. After a period of negative rates reflecting de-risking, a move toward positive funding would signal a pivot from deleveraging to aggressive positioning. This technical shift would confirm that the large pool of stablecoin liquidity is beginning to flow back into the market, potentially fueling the next leg up.

RALEIGH, NC / ACCESS Newswire / March 19, 2026 / ACCESS Newswire Inc. (NYSE American:ACCS), a leading communications company, today reported its operating results for the three months and full year ended December 31, 2025.
Foto: Accesswire "Our Q4 results reflect strong operational discipline as gross margins expanded to 77% and adjusted EBITDA amounted to $0.9M, or 15% of revenue. While we focused on a leaner business, we simultaneously launched Access Verified, our AI-powered optimizer, and we expect to launch our social monitoring platform, with our industry-leading AI Interactive Distribution Report before the end of March. Beginning in Q2 2026, we anticipate generating incremental revenue through premium subscription tiers and per-release pricing for these new offerings," said Brian R. Balbirnie, ACCESS Newswire's Founder and Chief Executive Officer.
Mr. Balbirnie continued, "As the only publicly traded independent newswire, we believe our agility and lean corporate structure are among our greatest competitive advantages. Combined with our momentum from our university program, where over 1,800 students across 60-plus universities have been trained on our ACCESS PR platform in just the past 90 days, we are positioning ourselves to be where we believe the market is going. We entered 2026 with clear product roadmap and a stronger margin profile and plan to focus on turning operational discipline into innovation, growth and sustained profitability."
Fourth Quarter 2025 Highlights:
Revenue - Total revenue for Q4 2025 was $5.8M, consistent with Q4 2024 and an increase of 1% compared to $5.7M in Q3 2025. The increase in revenue compared to the prior quarter is primarily due to an increase in average revenue per release due to the mix of releases disseminated as well as an increase in revenue from our webcasting business.
Gross Margin - Gross margin for Q4 2025 was $4.5M, or 77% of revenue, compared to $4.4M, or 75% of revenue, in Q4 2024 and $4.3M, also 75% of revenue in Q3 2025. The increase in gross margin is primarily due to lower employee costs due to optimization of our operational teams.
Operating Loss - Operating loss was $0.8M for Q4 2025, as compared to $14.3M during Q4 2024. The primary reason for the decrease in operating loss was due to an impairment charge recorded in Q4 2024 related to the Newswire tradename of $14.15M. Absent the impairment charge, operating expenses increased $0.4M, or 10%. This increase is primarily due to one-time charges related to a contract settlement as well as increased advertising and tradeshow expenses to promote our new branding.
Loss from continuing operations - On a GAAP basis, net loss from continuing operations was $0.5M, or $0.13 per diluted share, for Q4 2025, compared to $10.9M, or $2.85 per diluted share, for Q4 2024. As noted, the primary reason for the decrease in loss from continuing operations was due to the impairment charge recorded in Q4 2024, which was $10.7M, net of income tax expense.
Non-GAAP Measures - Q4 2025 EBITDA was $0.3M, or 4% of revenue, compared to $0.8M, or 13% of revenue, during Q4 2024. Adjusted EBITDA was $0.9M, or 15% of revenue, for Q4 2025 consistent with Q4 2024. Non-GAAP net income for Q4 2025 was $0.7M, or $0.17 per diluted share, compared to $0.8M, or $0.21 per diluted share, during Q4 2024. Adjusted free-cash flow was $0.5M for Q4 2025 compared to $0.4M for Q4 2024.
Full year 2025 Highlights:
Revenue - Total revenue was $22.6M for the full year of 2025, a 2% decrease from $23.1M during the full year of 2024. The decrease is primarily related to a decrease in revenue from our PRO plan products and webcasting and events business, partially offset by an increase in revenue from our core press release business driven by increases in subscriptions.
Gross Margin - Gross margin for the full year of 2025 was $17.3M, or 77% of revenue, compared to $17.4M, or 76% of revenue, during the full year of 2024. As noted for the quarter, gross margin was impacted by lower employee costs due to optimization of our operational teams, partially offset by increased distribution costs as we continue to invest in our distribution partners.
Operating Loss - Operating loss was $1.9M, for 2025, as compared to $16.3M during 2024. The decrease in the operating loss is primarily due to the previously noted impairment charge of $14.15M recorded during 2024.
Loss from continuing operations - On a GAAP basis, net loss from continuing operations was $1.6M, or $0.40 per diluted share during 2025, compared to $13.3M, or $3.47 per diluted share during 2024.
Non-GAAP Measures - EBITDA for full year of 2025 was $1.3M, or 6% of revenue, compared to $0.8M, or 4% of revenue, during 2024. Adjusted EBITDA was $3.2M, or 14% of revenue, for the full year of 2025 compared to $1.8M, or 8% of revenue, for 2024. Non-GAAP net income for the full year of 2025 was $2.2M, or $0.57 per diluted share, compared to $0.7M, or $0.19 per diluted share, during 2024. Adjusted free-cash flow was $1.3M for the full year of 2025 compared to $2.8M for 2024. Adjusted free-cash flow for 2025 included $2.2M of tax payments primarily related to gain on sale of the compliance business.
Key Performance Indicators:
As of December 31, 2025, we had 12,802 customers who had an active contract during the past twelve months.
Subscription customers increased during the quarter to 1,019, of which, 45 new subscribers came from our EDU platform as of December 31, 2025.
Average ARR for subscriptions per customer at the end of the quarter was $12,534, which does not include EDU customers, up from $10,844 as of December 31, 2024.

These measures, which are referred to as non-GAAP financial measures, are not prepared in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles in the United States, or GAAP. Our management uses these non-GAAP financial measures as tools for financial and operational decision making and for evaluating our own operating results over different periods of time.
EBITDA from continuing operations is calculated by excluding depreciation and amortization, interest expense, net, and income taxes from the loss from continuing operations. Adjusted EBITDA also excludes certain other expenses which the Company believes to be non-recurring as well as the gain or loss on the change in fair value of our interest rate swap. Non-GAAP net income (loss) from continuing operations is calculated by excluding stock-based compensation expense and amortization expense for acquisition-related intangible assets from loss from continuing operations and certain other adjustments noted in the tables below. Non-GAAP net income (loss) from continuing operations per share is calculated by dividing non-GAAP net income (loss) from continuing operations by the weighted-average diluted shares outstanding as presented in the calculation of GAAP net income (loss) from continuing operations per share. Because of varying available valuation methodologies, subjective assumptions and the variety of equity instruments that can impact a company's non-cash expenses, management believes that providing non-GAAP financial measures that exclude stock-based compensation expense allows for more meaningful comparisons between its operating results from period to period. For business combinations, management generally allocates a portion of the purchase price to intangible assets. The amount of the allocation is based on estimates and assumptions made by management and is subject to amortization. The amount of purchase price allocated to intangible assets and the term of its related amortization can vary significantly and are unique to each acquisition and thus management does not believe they are reflective of ongoing operations.
Free cash flow, a non-GAAP measure, represents cash flow from operating activities less purchase of property and equipment and capitalized software. Adjusted free cash flow also deducts certain cash payments which the Company believe to be non-recurring in nature. Management considers free cash flow and adjusted free cash flow to be liquidity measures that provide useful information to investors about the amount of cash generated or used by the business.

Bitcoin Reclaims $70,000 as Middle East Energy Strikes Trigger Flight to Safety
Jax MercerReviewed by
Shunan Liu
Bitcoin's price climbed to a 5-week high, surpassing $74,157 amid heightened geopolitical tensions and institutional accumulation. The surge came as large wallets increased their share of the total supply and U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs attracted significant inflows. Market participants are monitoring the asset's performance ahead of the Federal Reserve's upcoming rate decision.
Tensions in the Middle East have fueled a flight to safe-haven assets, with outperforming gold and the S&P 500. Improved geopolitical conditions and easing oil market concerns have contributed to the rally. Analysts note that Bitcoin's price movements are closely tied to macroeconomic developments and risk sentiment.
Corporate activity in the crypto space is also intensifying. Ferrari has suspended car deliveries in the Middle East due to the ongoing war, while defense firms like KNDS are engaging with regional clients on counter-drone solutions. South Korea's financial regulator has urged firms to enhance risk management amid the crisis.
How Did Markets React?
Bitcoin's price climbed above $75,000 as institutional demand for the asset grew. Companies like and Metaplanet are making large purchases, with Strategy acquiring 22,337 BTC for $1.57 billion. This activity suggests continued long-term conviction in Bitcoin as a store of value.
Retail investors are also shifting capital into Bitcoin, driven by expectations of further volatility due to geopolitical tensions. The asset's outperformance over traditional safe-haven assets like gold has reinforced this trend.
Bitcoin derivatives markets also saw significant movement, with $344 million in bearish positions liquidated in 24 hours. This suggests growing confidence in the asset's upward trajectory, at least in the near term.
What Are Analysts Watching Next?
Analysts are closely watching Bitcoin's performance ahead of the Federal Reserve's rate decision, expected later this week. The outcome of this meeting could influence risk appetite and capital flows across asset classes.
The broader crypto ecosystem is also evolving. BTQ Technologies has deployed BIP 360 on its Bitcoin Quantum Testnet v0.3.0, advancing post-quantum cryptography development. Regulatory timelines for quantum-safe systems are accelerating globally, with the U.S. targeting a 2026 deadline.
Institutional infrastructure for tokenized assets is also expanding. Flow Traders has launched 24/7 liquidity for tokenized stocks, gold, and money market funds, offering round-the-clock exposure management for institutional investors. This development highlights the growing role of crypto in traditional finance.
Bitcoin Everlight has also launched its presale, offering BTC-denominated rewards to participants. The project aims to reward node activity and transaction routing, operating independently of Bitcoin price fluctuations. With a fixed supply of 21 billion tokens and a focus on operational incentives, the project is attracting attention in the DeFi space.
Coinbase's stock has rebounded from a sharp Q1 2026 drop, as stablecoin volumes and Bitcoin prices have recovered. The firm is likely to exceed its Q1 guidance as USDC activity rebounds to record levels.
Thailand's political landscape remains stable as Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul was reelected following his party's victory in recent elections. However, the global energy crisis is expected to weigh on Thailand's economy.

H&R Block is uniquely qualified with online and in-person tax services to provide expert guidance and free services to ensure hourly wage earners keep as much of what they've earned as possible. For in-person expertise, taxpayers can visit one of 9,000 H&R Block offices to get support from a tax professional trained on the latest tax laws to ensure a maximum refund with personalized guidance.** For those who have already filed, a Second Look review is available to ensure the accuracy of previously filed returns, regardless of how they were filed.
“The opportunity is real, but so is the complexity,” said Andy Phillips, VP of the H&R Block Tax Institute. “When tax rules change, the risk is missing savings. We’re here to help taxpayers understand their options and claim every dollar they qualify for.”

label: marketscreener.com;US weekly jobless claims unexpectedly fall amid low layoffs | MarketScreener Saudi Arabia;https://sa.marketscreener.com/news/us-weekly-jobless-claims-unexpectedly-fall-amid-low-layoffs-ce7e5ededa80fe21;2026-03-19T12:41:00+00:00
text:
WASHINGTON, March 19 (Reuters) - The number of Americans filing new applications for unemployment benefits unexpectedly fell last week, pointing to stable labor market conditions and a rebound in job growth in March.
Initial claims for state unemployment benefits dropped 8,000 to a seasonally adjusted 205,000 for the week ended March 14, the Labor Department said on Thursday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast 215,000 claims for the latest week.
The government introduced new seasonal factors for 2026 and revised the seasonal factors from 2021 through 2025. Seasonal factors are the model used to strip out seasonal fluctuations from the series. Claims data was revised from 2021 through 2025.
Layoffs have remained relatively low even as businesses have been reluctant to increase headcount because of what economists said was uncertainty caused by President Donald Trump's sweeping tariffs. The Trump administration's immigration crackdown, which reduced labor supply, had also hampered job growth, they said.
The U.S. Supreme Court struck down the duties, pursued under a law meant for use in national emergencies, but Trump has imposed a 10% global tariff, which he said would rise to 15%. Investigations have been launched against some trade partners, which economists said would result in more tariffs.
Businesses also face more uncertainty from the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, which has boosted oil prices by more than 40% since the conflict started at the end of February.
The Federal Reserve on Wednesday kept its benchmark overnight interest rate in the 3.50%-3.75% range. Policymakers projected higher inflation, a steady unemployment rate and only a single reduction in borrowing costs this year.
The claims data covered the period during which the government surveyed businesses for the nonfarm payrolls component of March's employment report.
Payrolls decreased by 92,000 jobs in February, the sixth decline since January 2025 and the second largest.
Harsh winter weather, a strike by healthcare workers and payback following outsized payroll gains in January accounted for part of the decline. The weather drag likely faded in March and healthcare employees have returned to work, which should underpin job growth this month.
Nonetheless, employment growth has almost stalled, with Fed Chair Jerome Powell telling reporters on Wednesday that "you have got a sort of zero employment growth equilibrium," adding that "it does have a feel of downside risk, and it's not kind of a really comfortable balance."
The number of people receiving unemployment benefits after an initial week of aid, a proxy for hiring, increased 10,000 to a seasonally adjusted 1.857 million during the week ended March 7, the claims report showed.
Many unemployed people, including recent college graduates, are experiencing long spells of joblessness. The unemployment rate increased to 4.4% in February from 4.3% in January.
(Reporting by Lucia Mutikani; Editing by Chizu Nomiyama)

text:
Duluth Holdings tops Q4 expectations but issues softer FY2026 outlook; shares climb
Duluth Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:DLTH) reported fourth-quarter results that beat analyst forecasts, although its revenue outlook for fiscal 2026 came in below Wall Street expectations. Despite the cautious guidance, the company’s shares rose about 6.9% in premarket trading following the announcement.
The workwear and casual apparel retailer posted adjusted earnings per share of $0.23 for the quarter ended February 1, 2026, exceeding the analyst consensus estimate of $0.15 by $0.08. Revenue totaled $215.9 million, ahead of the $210.65 million forecast but down 10.5% compared with $241.3 million in the same quarter a year earlier.
Gross margin improved sharply to 53.0%, up from 44.1% in the prior-year period—an increase of 890 basis points—even after absorbing a $7.6 million impact from tariffs. The margin expansion was driven by higher average selling prices resulting from reduced promotional activity, along with lower product costs tied to the company’s direct-to-factory sourcing strategy.
For fiscal 2026, Duluth expects revenue in the range of $540 million to $560 million. The midpoint of $550 million is below the analyst consensus estimate of $559.9 million. The company also projects adjusted EBITDA between $26 million and $30 million, with capital expenditures of roughly $12 million.
“I couldn’t be prouder of the team’s disciplined efforts in managing promotional resets, controlling expenses, streamlining operations, and optimizing inventory levels,” said President and CEO Stephanie Pugliese.
Duluth reported net income of $7.8 million for the quarter, representing a $13.4 million improvement compared with the net loss of $5.6 million recorded in the fourth quarter a year earlier. Inventory declined 21.1% year over year, while full-year free cash flow reached $16.6 million—an increase of $41.8 million compared with the prior year.
Direct-to-consumer net sales dropped 16.5% to $144.3 million due to lower customer traffic, while retail store net sales rose 4.7% to $71.6 million, supported by the opening of two new locations. At the end of the quarter, the company held $16.3 million in cash and reported total net liquidity of $141.3 million.

“Adjustable-rate mortgages are offering meaningful savings in 2026’s expensive housing market,” said Bill Banfield, chief business officer at Rocket. “Even though housing costs have recently come down a bit, it remains tough for first-time buyers to break in—and for existing homeowners to walk away from their ultra-low rates. With ARMs providing borrowers with the biggest discount in nearly four years, choosing an ARM could be a gamechanger, saving buyers hundreds of dollars each month and thousands over a few years. ARMs typically make sense when rates are high enough that buyers don’t want to lock them in—like now. When rates are low, like they were during the pandemic, it’s worth locking them in for as long as possible.”
The benefit of a 30-year fixed rate mortgage, even when rates are fairly high, is that borrowers know exactly what their payment will be for the entire length of the loan. In today’s market, ARMs are offering lower payments during the initial period, but they come with some uncertainty. After the initial fixed-rate period, rates may be higher, pushing up monthly payments. Of course, rates could also be lower when the seven-year period ends.
ARMs Aren’t As Risky As They Used to Be
The ARM discount is big enough that buyers taking out a mortgage should talk to their lender about whether it’s a good option. ARMs can be a smart strategy for borrowers who plan to stay in a home only for the short term, have the financial means to afford a higher payment and/or plan to refinance their loan later. There’s a fairly good chance rates will fall enough during the fixed-rate period that it makes sense to refinance.
ARMs are not nearly as risky as they once were; new rules went into effect after the financial crisis to protect borrowers. One, ARMs come with interest-rate caps, which limit how much the rate can increase each term and over the life of the loan. Two, borrowers often have to qualify for an ARM based on a higher rate, so they typically have leftover room in their budget if the rate does increase. The typical mortgage lasts between four and seven years before the borrower refinances or sells, according to the National Mortgage Database; often, a homebuyer who takes on an ARM with a seven- or 10-year fixed rate period never even gets to the adjustable-rate period.

label: mirrorreview.com;Micron Technology Earnings Triples To $23.8B On Surging AI Memory Demand;https://www.mirrorreview.com/news/micron-technology-earnings-triples/;2026-03-19T11:43:00+00:00
text:
Mirror Review
March 19, 2026
Micron Technology reported that its revenue surged to $23.86 billion in Q2 FY2026 , nearly three times higher than $8.05 billion a year ago .
The reason behind the tripled Micron Technology earnings is an unprecedented demand for memory chips.
As companies invest billions into AI data centers, they need more high-performance memory. Micron is right at the center of that demand.
What Drove Micron Technology Earnings Growth
The sharp rise in Micron Technology earnings shows a shift in how computing works today.
Here are the key drivers:
AI data centers expansion : Tech giants are scaling AI infrastructure rapidly High-bandwidth memory demand : Critical for training and running AI models Tight supply conditions : Limited suppliers pushing prices higher Improved pricing power : Higher demand led to stronger margins Micron is one of only three global players dominating this space, alongside Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.
This limited competition has helped the company achieve record margins of over 74% , a rare figure in the traditionally cyclical memory industry.
Looking ahead, Micron expects:
Q3 revenue : ~$33.5 billion Gross margin : ~81% EPS : ~$19 These numbers show that the AI-driven momentum is not slowing down anytime soon.
“Memory Is Now A Strategic Asset”
Leadership at Micron made it clear that this is not just a short-term spike.
Sanjay Mehrotra said: “In the AI era, memory has become a strategic asset for our customers.”
This statement reflects that memory chips were once seen as commodity products. Today, they are becoming essential infrastructure for AI systems.
Why Micron Stock Still Fell
Despite record-breaking results, Micron’s stock dropped around 4% in premarket trading .
At first glance, this looks surprising. Strong earnings usually push stocks higher. But investors are looking beyond the present.
The concern is Micron’s aggressive spending.
2026 capex increased by $5 billion Total planned investment exceeds $25 billion Further increase expected in 2027
This expansion push is already underway. Micron Technology recently acquired a Taiwan chip facility from PSMC to scale its DRAM production capacity.
This level of spending signals confidence. But it also raises a familiar fear in the semiconductor industry.
Industry-Wide Impact
Following the earnings, shares of major memory players also declined:
Samsung fell around 3.8% SK Hynix dropped about 4% Even US storage firms like Western Digital and Seagate saw declines.
This signals a broader market concern. The issue is not the demand today, but what happens when everyone expands at the same time.
A Turning Point For The Semiconductor Industry
The current Micron Technology earnings highlight a key transition.
Memory is no longer just a commodity AI has turned it into critical infrastructure Profitability has reached historic highs But at the same time:
Capital spending is rising sharply Future supply risks are building This creates a unique moment where opportunity and risk are both at their peak.
End Note
The latest Micron Technology earnings show how deeply AI is reshaping the semiconductor industry.
Revenue has tripled, margins are at record levels, and demand continues to surge.
Yet, the market reaction tells a different story. Investors are not questioning today’s performance. They are questioning tomorrow’s sustainability.
Micron is making a bold bet that AI demand will continue to grow. If that bet holds, this could mark a new era for memory chips. If not, history suggests the cycle could turn again.
Maria Isabel Rodrigues

The Johannesburg and London dual-listed bank and wealth manager guided adjusted earnings per share of 81.6p to 84p, representing growth of 3% to 6% on the prior year, while headline EPS was expected to be broadly flat to 2% higher at 72.6p to 74.1p.
Basic EPS was forecast to rise between 6% and 9% to 76.9p to 79.2p.
Pre-provision adjusted operating profit is expected to increase by 3% to 5% to between £1.07bn and £1.09bn, while adjusted operating profit before tax was projected at £940.3m to £965.9m, compared with £920.0m in 2025.
The group said performance for the 11 months ended 28 February was driven by higher lending volumes, increased client activity and positive inflows into funds under management, partly offset by margin compression linked to declining global interest rates.
Within specialist banking, core loans rose to £36.3bn, representing growth of 7.4% on a currency-neutral basis, while customer deposits increased to £45.5bn.
Funds under management in the Southern African wealth business climbed 26.7% to £29.6bn, supported by strong discretionary inflows and a strategic acquisition in Switzerland.
The Southern African division was expected to deliver at least 4% growth in adjusted operating profit in rand terms, with the specialist bank growing at least 5% and maintaining a credit loss ratio at the lower end of its through-the-cycle range.
Return on equity for the region was projected at around 18%, within its medium-term target range.
In the UK, adjusted operating profit was expected to be broadly in line with the prior year, although the UK specialist bank is forecast to see a decline of between 1% and 5%.
Credit losses in the UK were expected to be at the upper end of guidance, while return on tangible equity is projected at between 13.3% and 13.7%.
Group return on equity was expected to be between 13.3% and 13.7%, with return on tangible equity of 15% to 16%, both within medium-term targets.
The group reiterated its ambition to move returns towards the upper end of those ranges by 2030.
Investec also confirmed completion of its £110m share buyback programme announced in May, supported by strong capital generation.
Revenue growth during the period was underpinned by higher average lending balances, increased fee income from banking activities and stronger annuity revenues in wealth management.
Elevated client hedging activity amid market volatility also supported trading income, while the group’s share of earnings from associate Rathbones increased year-on-year.
The group said it continued to invest in its corporate mid-market and private client franchises, as well as in technology and digital platforms, contributing to fixed cost growth alongside regulatory and strategic initiatives.
Investec said it maintained robust capital and liquidity positions, with CET1 ratios of 14.2% for Investec Limited and 12.3% for Investec plc at the end of December, supporting its strategy to grow market share, deepen client relationships and enhance long-term shareholder returns.
Full-year results for the year ending 31 March were scheduled to be released on 21 May.
